title: Thousand Suns: Using AI to build a nuclear war sandbox without giving up control
author: galantrixgames
selftext:
https://i.redd.it/95do5yst8u0i1.png

Hi there, r/aigamedev! I’ve just [released my free game Thousand Suns](https://galantrixgames.itch.io/thousand-suns) on [itch.io](http://itch.io), and I wanted to talk about my AI-enhanced development process. I see a lot of great posts here with games mostly, if not completely, built by AI (“vibecoded”), so I wanted to share my process, which was augmented by AI but still largely human-driven.

I’m an ex-Big Tech software engineer, so I have decades of programming experience. I’m now a stay-at-home dad and solo game developer who’s concerned about the dangers of nuclear weapons, so I decided to start building an ultra-realistic simulation/game hybrid just before the Iran war started. I built it full-time when I was not busy with parenting/household chores. At the time, I didn’t even have a paid AI subscription, so I bummed the free tiers across Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude.

I started with a *lot* of reading. Instead of reading the 20+ digital books I have on nuclear war, I just fully read a handful and used Gemini’s “Notebook” feature to allow quick consultation on the others. AI helped a lot when I wanted to double check one book’s conclusions with other sources, like “What do experts think about X”, so Gemini would check the other books for alternative viewpoints.

I then moved to prototyping, which was where I used AI very heavily to teach me how to use 3D in Godot. While I was already familiar with 3D development and Godot 2D development (from my previous game, [Outsider](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3040110/Outsider/)), Gemini Free was instrumental in teaching me some Godot 3D practices. I would basically use chat prompts and paste+modify code, all hacky throwaway stuff. Thousand Suns makes very heavy use of line shaders, so Gemini Free created an initial rough version and we worked together in keeping only what I’d need for the project. I actually challenged myself to delete every AI comment and come back a few days later to write one comment per shader line. I’d then run my comments by Gemini to see whether they were correct. This ensured that I really understood the purpose of every line and optimized the shader while at it.

I then moved to the $20 subscriptions, one provider at a time. Thousand Suns needed detailed population maps and country boundary data to estimate nuclear war casualties. These are all available online, but in formats hardly suitable for direct game use. I used a mix of QGIS to pre-process files plus Claude to write converters to my desired format. For instance, the original population map was a massive floating point array and I needed to both *resample* the map and bring it down to truncated 16-bit ushorts for a smaller memory footprint. I was at all times testing my prototypes on an old Core i5 laptop with iGPU to test performance and that made a huge difference. These converters were mostly written by Claude and perhaps the only area where I used AI *through desired outcomes rather than desired implementation*.

A critical part of the code was the nuclear damage calculation, which you can find on sites like NUKEMAP. Instead of asking AI to “vibe-convert” that code into C#, I went to the original sources and used Claude to help me find the right equations in the seminal work on the topic, Glasstone & Dolan’s “The Effect of Nuclear Weapons”. AI was only partially helpful here in a way that highlighted one of AI’s key limitations: it has a hard time discerning what is useful from what isn’t. It states with absolute certainty that I’d need to use certain equations that would be very hard to actually integrate in my simulation. The book is available as an old black and white scan and Claude had a really hard time reading graphs. So I did this manually and used AI to help me create the damage equations through linear regression - unlike NUKEMAP, which apparently interpolates from cached data points. The formulas went into an Excel spreadsheet that became the source of truth for the calculations and AI never touched that file. I converted the formulas manually into C#.

Thousand Suns is an event-based simulation, an approach I learned from Claude in a design discussion. The event queue/dispatcher is a central part of this approach and I wrote the first version manually, later making improvements with AI. This ensured that my mental model remained intact while letting go of the more tedious tasks such as refactoring data structures.

The simulation evolved gradually following this exact pattern: I’d write the first two or three versions and then grow them with AI. This reflected my overall philosophy for this project: I want AI to save me time but *never to do something I couldn’t or wouldn’t do myself*. I’m not saying that Claude didn’t have good ideas, but I still rejected many of them throughout development because they went against my design principles. Oftentimes, Claude would “admit” that my approach was better and they were wrong.

At this point I was using AI in around 50% of commits; it was writing most tests and reviewing everything I wrote. *If there’s something that AI is great at, it is analyzing code*. It found incredible and subtle bugs, saving me weeks of development.

I then switched to ChatGPT, and I was really impressed with 5.5 Sol and 6.1 Sol. I don’t think it’s necessarily better than Claude, but it has a fantastic cost-benefit. I had to steer it a bit more often, but it worked great as a fast workhorse. As with Claude, my AI-heavy commits never involved changing more than 100 lines or so. This is how I ensured that my mental model remained intact and that AI wasn’t messing up my project. On average, I made manual changes to 70-80% of the commits that involved AI code.

I’ve heard many times that AI is like a junior engineer and that’s also what I’ve observed. It’s like an immature savant: it knows a lot, it’s really “smart” and fast, but it does a bad job at managing complexity and ensuring design “normalization”. Without close supervision, complexity and hacks would start spreading around like a cancer and then suddenly *vibecoding would remain the only option left because you would no longer understand the project*.

With the simulation core and all the weapon, bomber and missile simulation code in place, I could go to graphics. I had decided to develop the entire simulation as if it supported *headless mode*: it is, in theory, able to calculate the full outcome of a nuclear war without displaying a single pixel on the screen. This separation, which I enforced with great vigor against Claude/ChatGPT’s hacks, paradoxically made continuing the project with AI a lot easier!

The model rendering layer (aka “graphics”) used a lot more AI than the lower layers because it’s kind of dumb. I’d provide my manually-created vector graphics, some data structures, write a bare version of the routines, and then have AI fill in the details. I don’t want to minimize this because this part can be very error prone, despite the low algorithmic complexity. That saved me a lot of time and sanity looking up “how to do X in Godot”.

I then reworked the file loading routines so the simulation could be fully data-centric. I wrote the documentation for all the files in the files themselves, populated them with comma-delimited data, wrote a loader for a couple of data types and asked AI to do the rest. This is one part where my job was mostly reviewing ChatGPT.

The simulation was already working great with graphics at this point, but I needed a UI. I designed the UI using Godot’s UI builder and asked AI to add handlers for buttons, drop downs, labels, etc. Things like “I want the Death display to read the models’ death count every frame” saved me from dealing with this also very boring piece of code.

At this point, already close to the end, AI was doing 60-70% of the coding but I was hardly worried about it. The commits were small, fast, easy to review and I could do many per day. “Now disable that control when X happens in the model”. I was feeling that I was “streaming mental code to the source files” by using AI. It was like ChatGPT was my keyboard and not an AI anymore because it was doing almost no “thinking”.

Throughout development, I never used more than 20-30% of my $20/month plan, especially after switching to ChatGPT. The amount of time saved with a few dollars per month was incredible. At the same time, my finished project fully reflects my mental model rather than just my *intention*. I can explain every line of code because I’ve either written or approved every single one of them. And I wasn’t burned out because AI took care of some of the most odious pieces of coding. If you worked as a software engineer long enough, you know that most code is just documentation and boilerplate grind.

Perhaps my AI-assisted coding isn’t the future - but it’s at least the future I want to be in. Thousand Suns was coded by a better version of myself, like if I left bed every day as Clark Kent but coded as Superman. You won’t see me fully vibecoding anytime soon, but I’ll never go back to the old fully manual style of coding.

That’s long enough! If you have any questions, feel free to ask!
